Adult Grey rockcod (Lepidonotothen squamifrons) are relatively large-bodied nototheniids, with field surveys indicating that individuals can attain a maximum total length of 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters]. This size is achieved after many years of slow, sustained growth in the frigid waters of the Southern Ocean. Estimates derived from otolith readings suggest that the maximum lifespan for this species is 19 years [am = 19 years] at 1.7 °C [T = 1.7 °C], a longevity that is not unusual among high-latitude notothenioids and reflects the profoundly low metabolic demands associated with a life spent at stable, subzero temperatures. This extended lifespan, coupled with delayed maturation, is a common life-history strategy among Antarctic fishes, allowing them to buffer the interannual variability in food supply that characterizes their pelagic ecosystem. The protracted juvenile phase, during which individuals must avoid predation while building sufficient energy reserves, represents a critical window that shapes population dynamics and recruitment success in this commercially harvested species.

Sexual maturation in Grey rockcod occurs at a relatively modest size compared to the species' ultimate length. Data from trawl surveys and histological analyses of gonadal tissue indicate that puberty is attained at a total length of 37.5 centimeters [Lp = 37.5 centimeters]. The corresponding body mass at this developmental milestone has been calculated from length-weight regressions specific to this population, yielding a wet weight at puberty of approximately 589 grams [Wwp = approximately 589 grams]. This mass represents a substantial somatic investment before the onset of reproductive activity. The energetic cost of gonad development is considerable, and females must allocate significant resources to the production of a large number of small, pelagic eggs. The onset of vitellogenesis is triggered by a combination of photoperiod cues and the attainment of a critical body condition, which ensures that only the largest and best-conditioned females participate in annual spawning events.

Reproductive output in Grey rockcod is characterized by a massive spawning effort, typical of many broadcast-spawning teleosts. Under the thermal conditions typical of their deep-water habitat, at a temperature of 1.7 °C [T = 1.7 °C], a single female can produce approximately 493 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 493 eggs per day] over the course of the spawning season. This high daily fecundity is achieved through a combination of batch spawning and continuous oocyte development. The eggs themselves are small, with a diameter of roughly 1.4 millimeters, and females typically spawn multiple times per season [F_R_i = multiple times per season]. Using the standard geometric relationship for a sphere, this egg size translates into a wet weight at birth for each individual offspring of just 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams]. This minuscule size at hatching is an adaptation to a pelagic larval existence, where a small body size facilitates drift with ocean currents and allows for the exploitation of microscopic planktonic prey.

The early life history of the Grey rockcod begins with a prolonged incubation period under the extreme cold of the Antarctic winter. The embryonic development within the egg is strongly temperature-dependent, and at the ambient temperature of -0.6 °C [T = -0.6 °C] typical of the species' spawning grounds, hatching occurs approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days] after fertilisation. This long incubation period is a direct consequence of the drastically slowed metabolic and enzymatic rates at subzero temperatures, a physiological constraint common to all high-latitude notothenioids. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva is entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves for nourishment during a period of several weeks, during which the mouth and digestive tract continue to develop. The transition to exogenous feeding coincides with the spring phytoplankton bloom, ensuring a reliable supply of copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton for the newly emerged larvae.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for Grey rockcod conforms to a power-law relationship with ultimate length, with the length-weight regression yielding an asymptotic wet weight of 2040 grams [Wwi = 2040 grams]. This mass places the species among the larger members of the genus Lepidonotothen, though it remains considerably smaller than the giant Antarctic toothfish. The combination of a 19-year maximum lifespan (19 years) [am = 19 years] and a substantial ultimate size allows this species to sustain a relatively low annual natural mortality rate, a demographic trait that makes it vulnerable to overfishing at a temperature of 1.7 °C [T = 1.7 °C]. The species' life history is finely tuned to the pulsed productivity of the Southern Ocean, with slow growth, deferred maturity, and a high fecundity representing adaptations to a variable environment where recruitment success is highly episodic. Understanding these parameters is essential for developing sustainable harvest strategies for this valuable fishery resource.
